summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for IEEE 802.3 repeater devices, which regenerate signals on Ethernet segments. It was replaced by RFC 1516.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of readings for the boxes that boost Ethernet signals, so network helpers can check them the same way across brands.

questions: how to manage ethernet repeaters with snmp
subtitle: SNMP management objects for Ethernet repeaters that amplify signals across segments

tldr.problem: Network administrators needed a standard way to monitor and manage IEEE 802.3 Ethernet repeaters, which amplify signals to extend network reach beyond a single cable segment.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Management Information Base (MIB) with SNMP objects describing repeater status, port configuration, activity monitoring, and MAC address tracking across physical groups and ports.
tldr.outcome: The standard unified management of repeaters across different vendors using SNMP, though it was superseded by RFC 1516 with enhanced definitions.

today: RFC 1368 was a Proposed Standard defining repeater management. It was superseded by RFC 1516, which provided additional and enhanced managed object definitions. The original repeater-based networking architecture has largely been replaced by switched Ethernet, making this RFC of historical interest.

sections.title: Repeaters and Ethernet Networks
sections.content:
An IEEE 802.3 repeater is a device that regenerates and amplifies electrical signals on Ethernet cables, allowing multiple cable segments to work as a single network. The repeater connects Ethernet segments together using ports, creating a star topology where every station on any connected segment can communicate with every other station.

A repeater is a bit-wise store-and-forward device: it forwards each bit of data it receives on one port to all other ports immediately, without making decisions based on packet content or addresses. This is different from bridges, which examine entire frames before deciding where to send them.
sections.plainLanguage: A repeater is like a megaphone for Ethernet cables. It listens for signals on one cable and shouts them out on all the other cables so the message reaches further.

sections.title: MIB Structure and Groups
sections.content:
The RFC defines a MIB module organized into three logical groups of managed objects. The Basic Group contains mandatory objects for all repeaters, including status and control information for the repeater itself, its port groups, and individual ports. The Monitor Group provides optional monitoring statistics such as collision counts and activity duration on each port. The Address Tracking Group tracks the MAC addresses of devices attached to repeater ports, allowing administrators to see which hosts are on which segments.

Each repeater can organize its ports into numbered groups, matching physical hardware divisions like plug-in cards in a modular chassis. Each group can contain up to 1024 ports, and each port within a group is uniquely identified by a combination of group number and port number. This grouping is optional but recommended for clarity in modular systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The checklist has three sections: how the whole repeater is doing, how busy each cable is, and which computers are plugged into which holes.

sections.title: Repeater Port Functions
sections.content:
The RFC defines seven functions that a repeater port uses to process incoming signals and manage data flow. The Collision Event Function detects when two or more signals arrive simultaneously and outputs a collision signal. The Carrier Event Function recognizes when valid data is arriving on a port. The Framing Function identifies frame boundaries by tracking the carrier signal and decoded data, stripping off the preamble and ensuring data aligns to byte boundaries.

The Activity Timing Function measures how long a carrier signal is present, in bit times. The Octet Counting Function counts the number of complete bytes received. The Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) Function verifies the frame check sequence to detect corruption. The Source Address Function extracts the source MAC address (bytes 7-12) from each frame. These functions work together to produce the counters and observations that the MIB objects expose to management applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The repeater listens carefully to each cable: it notices when two messages crash into each other, counts how many bits arrive, checks if the message is broken, and remembers who sent it.

sections.title: Managed Objects and Counters
sections.content:
The MIB defines objects for querying and controlling repeater behavior. Basic objects include rptrGroupCapacity (the maximum number of groups, up to 1024) and rptrGroupPortCapacity (the maximum ports per group). Objects exist for each group's operational status and the timestamp of the last change, allowing administrators to detect when hardware has been swapped out.

Port-level objects expose counters for collisions, activity duration, octet counts, framing errors, and frame check sequence errors. MAC address tracking objects record which source addresses have been seen on which ports. All of these objects are exposed through SNMP, allowing a management station to poll the repeater regularly and collect statistics, log trends, and raise alarms when problems are detected.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask the repeater: how many groups do you have? How many ports in each? How many collisions did port 3 see today? And which computer MAC addresses are hooked up where?

sections.title: Relationship to SNMP and MIB Standards
sections.content:
This MIB module is defined using the Structure of Management Information (SMI) from RFC 1155, and follows the naming and object definition conventions of RFC 1212. Objects are accessed via the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) defined in RFC 1157, which allows a management station to retrieve object values and, in some cases, set configuration parameters on the repeater.

The MIB assumes that any repeater implements this standard will also implement the mandatory 'system' group from MIB-II (RFC 1213). However, the repeater's ports are not modeled as network interfaces in the MIB-II sense; they are physical repeater ports that operate at the bit level, not at the packet level. The 'interfaces' group in MIB-II applies only to the management interface(s) through which the repeater is reached, not to the repeater's data ports themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: The repeater speaks the SNMP language so that management software can talk to it. It also knows the standard checklist format that all network gear uses.
